title.narrative: Utariri: Integrated Biodiversity, Climate and Livelihoods Programme
Utariri: Integrated Biodiversity, Climate and Livelihoods Programme

description.narrative:
Programmet syftar till att stärka lokala samhällens kapacitet och incitament att förvalta Zambezidalens landskap, nyttja naturresurser på ett hållbart sätt och säkerställa att även framtida generationer kan nyttja naturresurserna på samma sätt. Lokala samhällen kommer att få stöd för att diversifiera sina inkomstkällor, delta i ekonomin kring djur och natur, utföra klimatsmart jordbruk och minimera konflikt mellan människor, djur och natur.
Programmet har fyra strategiska mål: i) skydd, restaurering och förvaltning av naturresurser; ii) minimerad konflikt mellan människor, djur och natur; iii) förbättrade inkomstmöjligheter för lokala samhällen; och iv) stärkt kapacitet och kunskap hos involverade aktörer.

The programme sets out to empower communities to act as incentivised custodians of the Zambezi Valley landscape, sustainably utilising the natural resources around them while ensuring that future generations can derive the same benefits. Communities will be supported to diversify their income streams, participate in the wildlife economy, implement climate smart agriculture and reduce human-wildlife conflict.
The programme has four strategic objectives: i) natural resource protection, restoration and management; ii) reduction of human-wildlife conflict; iii) improved income earning opportunities for communities; and iv) stakeholder capacity building skills and knowledge.

Strategic Objectives of the Utariri Programme are
1. Natural resource protection, restoration and management
Outcome 1: Increased community stewardship and sustainable utilisation of natural resources focusing on pro-poor and gender sensitive empowerment actions.
This will be achieved through increased community stewardship focussing on pro poor and gender sensitive empowerment actions. The key programme activities will include a huge drive for reforestation and support for indigenous tree woodlots for over 1000 households and 20 local schools. Activities also include expanding the use of the Community Share Ownership Trust model which brings the communities, private sector and authorities to a roundtable to share burdens and profits associated with biodiversity management and builds on the extensive lessons learnt from the CAMPFIRE Programme. The key implementors in this objective will be DCA and AWF.
2. Reduction of Human Wildlife Conflict
Outcome 2: Enhanced ecological restoration and improved landscape planning for communities.
This will be achieved through improved landscape planning for communities. Programme activities will include careful landuse planning and positioning of strategic and solarised (where appropriate) water points for both communities and wildlife, use of chilli and beeehives as natural fences (these also create income earning potential), use of technology such as collaring animals and training and equipping of community-based scouts. The key implementors for this objective will be DCA, AWF and BAT.
3. Improved Income Earning Opportunities for Communities
Outcome 3. Enhanced participation of women and youths in livelihoods and resilience building efforts.
This will be achieved through multiplication and diversification of livelihood opportunities with a particular focus on inclusion of women and youth. Activities include promotion of agrobased activities that are climate smart and high value for example quinoa, amaranth, chillies and mushrooms as well as value chain strengthening of apiculture and non-timber forest products. Support will be in the form of starter kits, agro ecology training, establishing community associations for on and off farm products, developing logistics systems to enable online market linkages and promotion of tourism based local economies. The key implementors will be FACHIG and FOHF.
4. Stakeholder Capacity Building and Skills and Knowledge Transfer
Outcome 4. Increased gender sensitive public, private participation in sustainable biodiversity management, climate, and research.
The objective is to ensure that responsible authorities can meaningfully deliver their mandates and for increased gender sensitive public, private participation in natural resource management. Activities include supporting research work and innovations by local NGOs or community-based organisations working in biodiversity management, assisting Zimbabweans to participate in wildlife value chains and creating opportunities for women and youth to be paid custodians of the ecosystem. All consortium members will work in collaboration to achieve this objective.
Each consortium member brings specific expertise in at least one of the objective areas in a particular geography of the Zambezi Valley. The consortium partners will build each others capacity and complement each others work to achieve the ambitious targets set.

Background, including results during the second year of implementation The Utariri stewardship programme is being implemented in 4 districts in the Zambezi valley with the main objective to enhance ecosystem, biodiversity and livelihoods. The number of targeted households are 12 000(around 60 000 beneficiaries). The programme takes a landscape approach and is implemented by a consortium with the DanChurchAid in lead, together with Africa Wildlife Foundation, Bush life Africa Trust, FACHIG Trust, The Future of Hope Foundation, My Trees Trust. Despite the delayed start of implementation of the programme and the effect of the El Niño drought and climate change variability in 2024, political and economic challenges, the DCA and its implementing partners have shown their capacity in working towards the achievement of the planned results. All the funds have been disbursed, a total of 64 MSEK. So far, the Utariri programme has reached 9,355 households, with a target of 12,000 households.
Outcome 1: Increased community stewardship and sustainable utilization of natural resources focusing on propoor and gender sensitive empowerment actions. The community awareness sessions on biodiversity, stewardship and natural resources management have improved relations between stakeholders, relevant authorities and communities. These interventions have also seen communities taking the lead in various environmental management activities. Communities have a more positive attitude towards wildlife because they now understand that wildlife is part of the ecosystem. Some examples of results include: 150,348 indigenous tree seedlings were planted in Hurungwe over 127 hectares by 339 farmers (210F129M). The average survival rate was 78% which translates to 105,244 standing trees. 6 ESCs and Communitybased Wildlife Committees (a total of 526) committee members in Mbire district, were trained on the roles of the committee members, financial management and literacy, and identification of wardlevel projects/ interventions that the committees can embark on. 41 community scouts (18F 23M) conducted 30 sessions reaching 642 people (245M 397F) on Human WildlifeConflict.
Outcome 2: Enhanced ecological restoration and improved landscape planning for communities. Ecological restoration and protection of wildlife and habitats in the MidZambezi Valley landscape is gradually yielding impact. The training and equipping of community scouts by the project were complimented by Hurungwe RDC creating Quick Response Teams (QRTs). QRTs work with community scouts to respond to HWC reports. Water provision for domestic use led to the creation of household nutrition gardens for food security. Community water points established/resuscitated to mitigate water resource competition between humans and animals, for example: In Hurungwe, two (2) new boreholes were drilled and equipped with solarpowered pumping systems, providing six (6) tap stands for community water access, three (3) cattle troughs, reducing competition for water between livestock and wildlife. A total of seven (7) highyield boreholes were rehabilitated or upgraded to solarpowered PWS in wildlife conflictprone areas. In Muzarabani, rehabilitation of 16 water points for the community providing water to 657 households (3,285 individuals) and two schools, one clinic, and one business centre, ensuring broad access to potable water.
Outcome 3. Enhanced participation of women and youths in livelihoods and resilience building efforts. Various interventions to achieve food and income security in the four operational districts have been conducted e.g. introduction and an increase of sesame as an alternative cash crop to cotton in Muzarabani District was a welcome intervention. Use of agroecological production has benefitted farmers as they can now produce crops without the use of synthetic fertilizers thereby saving additional costs. Farmers now use bokashi, compost, liquid manure and treated manure which are all locally available resources for soil improvement. The adoption of agroecology by farmers was catalyzed using the Farmer Field School (FFS) approach and this saw a major shift in agronomical practices. Mushroom production proved pivotal in food and income security. 2,632 farmers (50 % female) were reached by Farmer Field Schools. Each farmer was provided with starter kits composed of sorghum, cowpea, groundnut, and a choice of sesame, chilies and quinoa was provided. Twenty ISALS groups each with 15 members were formed and trained by TFoHF in collaboration with Ministry of Women Affairs.
Outcome 4. Increased gender sensitive public, private participation in sustainable biodiversity management, climate, and research .The Utariri Fellowship Programme recruited 6 master level fellows from various disciplines and Universities in Zimbabwe and their research will feed into the Utariri project evidence gathering and interventions. The project supported 3 local NGOs, namely WCA, BIZ and CCAZ to undertake various project activities in the landscape. WCA was given funds to support the mitigation of humanwildlife conflict through installation of predatorproof mobile bomas in Mbire and Nyaminyami districts, and to pilot the adoption of apiculture as a livelihood in Nyaminyami District. 18 predator proof bomas protecting 117 cattle were deployed in Mbire and Nyaminyami districts and 80 community members (22F: 58M) benefited from the apiculture intervention in Nyaminyami.
Crisis Modifier results
The Crisis Modifier was implemented to mitigate the impact of El Niñoinduced drought in Hurungwe districts. A total of 2,030 households in wards 7, 8 and 9 were assisted with access to nutritious food for life saving purposes. In addition, total of 2,500 households were also supported with 2kg seed packs of sorghum, groundnut, and cowpea seeds. Together, these efforts have significantly alleviated the food insecurity situation in the district and has assisted in the recovery efforts of the affected targeted households. Most supported farmers reported a significant increase in crop yields specifically in sorghum and cowpeas helping them recover from the effects of the drought and improving their longterm resilience. The frequency and adoption of negative coping strategies diminished, with most households ceasing to employ such strategies by the second PDM. However, a few households with larger numbers of dependents continued to use these strategies, albeit to a lesser extent. The monthly entitlements have improved food access as it allows rights holders to purchase vegetable oil, cereals, and protein, although insufficient to enable targeted households to purchase other essential food groups such as dairy products, meat, fish, eggs, vegetables and fruits. In line with the government policy on food distribution, the crisis modifier was limited to specific MEB items, hence the dietary diversity score was skewed to medium. The reported results are in alignment with the observations made during the field visits to Hurungwe district, Kariba district and the Matusadona National Park in February 2025. During the field visit, the Embassy managed to visit different activities including crisis modifier (distribution of food through evouchers to vulnerable households), conservation clubs, water irrigation schemes, agroecology, irrigation, fungiculture, community production, reforestation, tree nurseries as well as presentation of African Parks/Matusadona Conservancy Trust. It was also reinsured that the consortium members have a local presence and with their own expertise and comparative advantages.
